title: Holy water at home
hook: a font by the door, used when leaving and returning

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Saint Michael prayer: protection by God's power, and never against flesh and blood. Your line was defend us in battle. Did you aim at the problem and not the person? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

A small cup screwed to the wall beside a front door, at shoulder height, between the light switch and the hook for keys. Sometimes it's a ceramic shell with a saint painted on it. Sometimes it's bone dry, because nobody remembered to refill it. A child heading out to school dips two fingers, touches forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other, and is out the door before the shape is finished. Today: the holy water font at home.
screen: `A CUP BY THE FRONT DOOR.` → `TWO FINGERS, A QUICK CROSS.` → `OUT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Begin at church. A Catholic walking into a church dips a hand in holy water at the door and makes the sign of the cross. The Church says it recalls baptism, the water a Christian first passed through. Now carry the font home. Families can ask a priest to bless water, take it home in a bottle, and fill a small font by the front door. The gesture from the church door now happens at the house door: going out to work, coming back from the hospital, leaving for a first date. Next, why the door. Thresholds are where a day changes direction. You walk out into hours you can't control and come back carrying whatever they gave you. A psalm has a verse for exactly this, in the Douay-Rheims: "May the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out; from henceforth now and for ever." The font turns that verse into a gesture. Third, the older prayer behind the water. Before the main Sunday Mass in the older Latin rite, the priest could walk through the church sprinkling the people while the choir sang Asperges me. The words come from a psalm of repentance, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed: thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow." Water at the front door says the same thing on a Tuesday morning: wash me, start me again. Last, what it isn't. Like a medal, the water isn't a force field. It doesn't keep accidents off the driveway. It's a sacramental: a sign, blessed by the Church's prayer, that turns a person toward God at the moment it's easiest to forget, hand on the doorknob, keys in hand, already late.
screen: `AT CHURCH: BAPTISM REMEMBERED.` · `A FONT BY THE FRONT DOOR.` · `KEEP THY COMING IN AND GOING OUT.` · `WASH ME, START ME AGAIN.` · then, large: `GOING OUT BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless yourself going out, and rehearse it here first. Let your feet rest on the floor. Think of the next door you'll walk through to leave: home, work, a classroom, a car. If you have holy water, you can set it where your hand will find it. If not, a sign of the cross at the threshold will do, or simply a pause with your hand on the handle. If you pray, you can borrow the psalm's words: May the Lord keep thy coming in and thy going out. If you don't, let the doorway be one breath before the day takes you. Rest now. The bell holds the time.
Holy water at home. Blessed water in a small font by the door, used for the sign of the cross going out and coming back: baptism remembered at the threshold. Today's word.
Your line: going out blessed. Today, every time you leave a building, pause for one second at the door before you step through. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics bless themselves with holy water at the church door, and some families keep a small font of blessed water by the front door at home, making the sign of the cross when leaving and returning.
